headline: Maine paid-leave program logs 8,376 applications in first report
dek: The new statewide benefit approved 4,720 claims during its first three months of data, while officials said the trust fund is projected to remain stable for the next decade.
body: Maine's new paid family and medical leave program received 8,376 applications during its first three months of claims activity, giving workers and employers the first detailed look at how the benefit is being used. The Maine Department of Labor published the figures Oct. 1 in the program's first claims administration report, alongside a new actuarial report that projects the program's trust fund will remain stable for the next 10 years. The claims period ran from March 30 through June 30, 2026, according to the department's [announcement](https://www.maine.gov/labor/news_events/article.shtml?id=13363661).

The early numbers are a launch snapshot, not a full-year measure. Workers could begin submitting applications March 30, but benefits became payable only for leave taken on or after May 1. Of the 8,376 submissions, 511 were later canceled and 682 were filed with the public administrator by workers covered by an approved private plan. Another 691 were still awaiting a decision when the data was pulled, leaving 6,492 decided claims. The report says the next annual report, due Oct. 1, 2027, will cover a full year from July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027.

Among the decided claims, 4,720, or 72.7%, were approved and 1,772, or 27.3%, were denied. The most common denial reason was missing documentation: 57.5% of denied claims fell into that category. Other denials involved earnings requirements, exhausted leave, identity verification, documentation that did not establish eligibility, or timing rules. The report says 6.7% of denials involved an identity that could not be verified, while some applications sought payment for leave before the May 1 benefit date. Those figures describe the first administrative experience and may change as workers, employers and the claims administrator become more familiar with the system.

Medical leave was the largest approved category. The report attributes 42.4% of approved claims to medical conditions other than pregnancy, 14.9% to pregnancy, 30.7% to bonding with a child through birth, adoption or foster care, and 11.6% to caring for a family member with a serious health condition. Safe leave accounted for 0.4% and military family leave for 0.1%. The average weekly benefit across approved claims was $816.33. Continuous leave made up 86.49% of approved claims, compared with 11.88% for intermittent leave and 1.63% for reduced schedules. These categories come from the [claims report](https://www.maine.gov/paidleave/docs/2026/ClaimsAdministrationAnnualReport2026.pdf).

The report also offers an early, limited demographic picture. Workers ages 26 to 41 submitted 54.3% of claims, the largest age group, followed by workers ages 42 to 57 at 23.4%. Women submitted 62.9% of claims, men 33.9%, and 0.4% came from applicants identifying as nonbinary; 2.8% did not provide a gender response. Race data was less complete: 58.8% of applicants declined to answer, while 38.6% selected White. The department cautions that the small initial data set can overrepresent particular circumstances and that future reports may shift those proportions.

Maine's program was created by a 2023 law and provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of paid leave for their own serious health condition, pregnancy, bonding with a new child, caring for a family member, qualifying military-family needs or safety-related leave. The Department of Labor administers the program, with Aflac handling claims administration, according to the report. The earlier [actuarial report](https://www.maine.gov/paidleave/docs/2025/MEPFMLActuaryReport.pdf) describes the funding structure: employers with at least 15 workers contribute 1% of wages and may deduct up to half from employees, while smaller employers contribute 0.5% and may deduct that full amount.

The new actuarial projection is intended to answer the program's central financial question as benefits begin: whether contributions and investment income can keep pace with claims and administration. Its baseline table projects a net fund balance of $304.5 million at the end of 2026, rising to $448.1 million at the end of 2036. Those are projections, not cash already held or a guarantee of future rates; they depend on assumptions about payroll, claims, benefits and expenses. The Department of Labor characterized the trust fund as solvent and stable for the next decade, while the claims report says the coming full-year data will provide a more useful test of early assumptions.

For Maine workers, the immediate practical takeaway is that the benefit is operating but documentation and plan eligibility matter. The department says workers, employers and self-employed people can get help through the program website and separate benefits and contributions portals. As more claims mature, the state will have to show whether processing times, approval patterns and the fund's projected cushion hold across a full year rather than a three-month launch period. Independent coverage by [The Maine Wire](https://www.themainewire.com/2026/10/nearly-5000-mainers-took-paid-family-leave-from-april-through-june/) likewise reported the first approval totals and benefit mix, while noting that the initial report is too short to settle longer-term questions about cost and use.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Maine paid-leave program logs 8,376 applications in first report
seoDescription: Maine's first paid family and medical leave report covers 8,376 applications, 4,720 approvals and a 10-year trust-fund projection.
